ood_note: const_in is a solver-generated in-distribution control; its error is the dataset-vs-solver floor (~1.44%) plus the surrogate's own error.

trust.card_note: informational only; Spearman with true error: 0.04 in range, 0.97 on OOD
trust.spread_html: Ensemble spread is shown as a raw number, not as a trust score. In-distribution it does not rank the true error (Spearman 0.04, p = 0.44); on the OOD set it does (0.97). Above 2.5e-04 (99th percentile of test spread) it flagged const_in 0%, const_high 100%, smooth 100%, noise 100%, pulse 100%, step 100% of the held-out OOD set, so read a large spread as 'unlike the training data', not as an error size.

explainer_html: Accurate solver (black): the PDEBench equations solved with an implicit BDF2/Newton scheme on the same 1024-cell grid; it agrees with a tight-tolerance reference to 2.4e-04 (relative L2) at the step used here. Dataset-style (orange): interpolation between stored PDEBench trajectories. The generator integrated with SciPy RK45 at default tolerances, which leaves a 1.45% relative-L2 time-integration error that grows with t. Surrogate (blue): trained on the dataset, so it reproduces the dataset (0.124% mean on held-out test samples) and inherits its offset from the accurate solution (1.44%). Shown only for spatially constant ICs at the training physics.
observables_html: The breakthrough curve at x = 1 is not shown: the outflow boundary u = D·∂u/∂x with D = 5e-4 keeps u(1) ≈ 0, so it is flat in every sample. Instead: the concentration at a chosen x, the position of the u = 0.5 front, and the total amount that has entered the column (uptake). The inflow flux at x = 0 is not shown either: it depends on 1 − u in the first cell, and even the PDEBench data differs from the accurate solver there by 22.54% (the surrogate: 19.63% vs data). Uptake is its time integral and is robust: ensemble vs data 0.113%.
footer_html: Ensemble: 5 × FNO (fno_pad0), trained on 3,200 PDEBench samples (keys 0000–3199); test keys 3600–3999. All numbers on this page come from results/*.json produced in this project.
model_guide_html: In range (flat IC, 0 < c < 0.2): interpolation wins. Interpolating stored trajectories in c is 0.009% from held-out data with all 3,200 training trajectories (0.051% with the 256-level table this app serves); the FNO ensemble is 0.124%. Out of distribution, the FNO ensemble is better for: const_high (8.62% vs 37.29%), smooth (2.90% vs 3.43%), pulse (6.79% vs 7.45%), step (6.81% vs 9.68%) (ensemble vs interpolation, against the accurate solver). Interpolation from the mean level is still better for: noise (2.15% vs 1.54%), because those ICs smooth out within the first output steps. Interpolation cannot extrapolate: above its table it clamps to the edge. The OOD set has only 6–8 samples per family, so small differences (e.g. smooth, pulse) are within noise.
two_errors_html: Two errors, always shown together: vs dataset is how well the model reproduces PDEBench's stored trajectories (what it was trained on); vs accurate solver is the error against the equations solved accurately. They differ by the dataset's own RK45 tolerance error (~1.44%).
padding_note: Padding comparison, 3 seeds each (mean ± std): test rel L2 pad0 0.129% ± 0.003% vs pad 0.25 0.135% ± 0.004%; right-boundary MAE 4.4e-04 vs 2.7e-04 (padding helps only there).
